unit.title: Commodities
unit.description: Gold, oil, metals and agricultural commodities: what moves them and how to invest in them

steps.title: Why people buy gold
steps.body:
Gold **pays no interest or dividends**. People buy it as a **safe haven**: in a crisis, against inflation or when they don't trust currencies. Central banks also stockpile it as a reserve.

Since it yields nothing, when **real interest rates** (after inflation) rise, holding gold "costs" more and it tends to suffer.

steps.title: It shines… now and then
steps.body:
• **1980:** a high of about $850 an ounce. It didn't beat that again until **2008**, and lost a lot of real value along the way.
• **2020:** a record above $2,000 in the middle of the pandemic.
• **2025:** it topped **$4,000** for the first time.

It can go decades without beating inflation.

steps.title: What it's for in a portfolio
steps.body: A small slice can help diversify because it sometimes rises when stocks fall. But it produces no income: its return depends only on what someone else will pay tomorrow.
steps.key: Gold sometimes protects you, but it produces nothing.
steps.tip: A safe haven that can go 20 years without rising is a risk too.

steps.title: Brent and WTI
steps.body:
There are two benchmark prices:

• **Brent:** North Sea crude, the benchmark in Europe.
• **WTI:** Texas crude delivered at Cushing (Oklahoma), the benchmark in the US.

They're priced in **dollars per barrel** (about 159 litres). That's why the dollar matters to Spain too.

steps.title: What moves it
steps.body:
• **Demand:** global growth, especially in the US and China.
• **Supply:** **OPEC** (founded in 1960) and, since 2016, **OPEC+**, with Russia and other producers, agree production quotas.
• **Geopolitics:** wars, sanctions, straits like Hormuz.
• **Inventories:** how much crude is in storage.

steps.title: Three historic shocks
steps.body:
• **1973:** the OPEC embargo quadrupled the price.
• **2008:** WTI came close to **$147** in July… and by December it was below $40.
• **20 April 2020:** with the world in lockdown, the May WTI contract closed at **−$37.63**: sellers were paying to have it taken off their hands.
steps.key: Oil moves on supply, demand and geopolitics, and it can do so violently.

steps.title: Metals that measure the economy
steps.body:
• **Copper:** cables, construction, electric cars. It's called **"Dr Copper"** because its price tends to anticipate how the economy is doing.
• **Aluminium, nickel, lithium:** industry and batteries.
• **Silver:** half jewellery, half industry: almost **60 %** of its demand in 2024 was industrial (electronics, solar panels).

steps.title: Agricultural: the weather rules
steps.body:
Wheat, maize, coffee, cocoa and sugar depend on **harvests, weather and wars**:

• **2022:** the invasion of Ukraine pushed Chicago wheat to 14-year highs. Russia and Ukraine accounted for about 30 % of global exports.
• **2024:** poor harvests in West Africa sent cocoa up **178 %** in the year.

steps.title: Much more volatile
steps.body: Agricultural commodities can double or crash because of a drought or a frost. They're also traded through futures, so investing in them isn't as simple as "buying coffee".
steps.key: Industrial metals: a thermometer for the economy. Agricultural commodities: weather and harvests.

steps.title: Four routes
steps.body:
• **Physical:** coins or bars. You own the metal, but you have to store it, and dealers charge a spread to buy and sell.
• **ETC** (*exchange traded commodity*): trades like an ETF; technically it's a debt security. Gold ETCs are usually **backed by physical metal**.
• **Futures:** contracts to buy or sell on a set date. Leveraged and complex.
• **Shares** in mining or oil companies.

steps.title: A company isn't the commodity
steps.body:
A gold miner earns more when gold rises, but it has **costs, debt and managers**: it usually moves more than the metal, both up and down. An oil company pays dividends; the barrel doesn't.

ETCs on oil or agricultural commodities use **futures**, and that has a hidden cost you'll see in the next lesson.

steps.title: Before you buy
steps.body: In Spain, ETCs are taxed when you sell, like ETFs: you can't switch between them without paying tax. Read the key information document and check whether the product is **physical** or tracks with **futures**.
steps.key: Investing in gold isn't the same as investing in a gold miner.

steps.title: The futures curve
steps.body:
A future fixes today the price of a barrel delivered later on, and each month has its own price:

• **Contango:** later futures are **more expensive** than nearer ones. It happens when there's too much crude: storing it costs money.
• **Backwardation:** later ones are **cheaper**. It happens when there's a shortage and everyone wants it now.

steps.title: The cost of rolling
steps.body:
An oil fund doesn't want to receive barrels: before the contract expires, it **sells the near one and buys the next**.

In contango it sells cheap and buys dear: with the same money it holds **fewer barrels** each month. Even if crude doesn't move, the fund loses.

steps.title: The 2020 case
steps.body: In April 2020 there was so much spare crude that the May WTI contract hit **−$37.63**, while the following ones were worth much more. The biggest US oil ETF (USO) **lost around 68 % in 2020**, while spot WTI fell around **20 %**.
steps.key: In contango, a futures fund can lose money even if crude goes up.
steps.tip: Before you buy a commodity product, check how it tracks the price.

steps.title: What it takes to recover
steps.body: Enter a 68 % fall: you'll see it takes a rise of more than 200 % to get back to where you started.

u15l1-1.prompt: Look at gold from 2018 to summer 2020. What trend do you see? (Gold · weekly closes · to 03/08/2020)
u15l1-1.explanation: From about $1,200 to over $2,000: fear, low rates and the pandemic pushed money into the safe haven.

u15l1-2.prompt: Tap gold's lowest point in this period. (Gold · weekly closes · to 03/08/2020)
u15l1-2.explanation: The low came at the end of 2018, at around $1,190. From there it rose around 70 % until August 2020.

u15l1-3.prompt: August 2020: gold has just set a record above $2,000 in the middle of the pandemic. What did it do over the following months?
u15l1-3.explanation: That summer nobody knew when vaccines would arrive or what real interest rates would do, and they're among the things that weigh most on gold.

u15l1-4.prompt: What does gold generate for its owner each year?
options: Nothing: no interest and no dividends
u15l1-4.explanation: You only make money if someone pays more tomorrow. That's why you can't value it with a P/E ratio.

u15l1-5.prompt: Gold hit a high in 1980 that it didn't beat again until 2008.
u15l1-5.explanation: About $850 an ounce in 1980. Taking inflation into account, anyone who bought at the peak lost a huge amount of purchasing power.

u15l1-6.prompt: Real chart of a commodity: 30 sessions with no name or date. What did it do over the next 10?
u15l1-6.explanation: Being a "safe haven" doesn't make an asset predictable in the short term: it has very volatile weeks too.

u15l1-7.prompt: What tends to favour gold? Select all that apply.
options: Very high and rising real rates
u15l1-7.explanation: With high real rates, a bond that pays something has the edge over an asset that pays nothing.

u15l1-8.prompt: Gold went from about $850 in 1980 to about $2,000 in 2020. How much did it rise in total (in %)?
u15l1-8.explanation: (2,000 − 850) ÷ 850 ≈ 135 % over 40 years: just over 2 % a year, below US inflation over that period.

u15l1-9.prompt: Quick: what usually happens to gold when real rates rise sharply?
u15l1-9.explanation: Holding an asset with no income gets more expensive compared with a bond that pays more.

u15l1-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: He's right, it's the perfect safe haven
Gold can go decades without rising; at most, a small slice to diversify
u15l1-10.explanation: No asset "never goes down". Gold diversifies, but it also has very long spells without rising.
feedback: Careful: it took 28 years to get back to its 1980 high.
OK: it's not a magic piggy bank, it's just one more piece of the portfolio.
It pays nothing: you only make money if the price goes up.
lines: My uncle says gold "never goes down" and I should put everything in it 🪙

u15l2-1.prompt: This is how WTI moved from mid-2019 to April 2020. What trend do you see? (WTI oil · weekly closes · to 20/04/2020)
u15l2-1.explanation: From over $50 to under $20 on a weekly close: the pandemic crushed demand just as Saudi Arabia and Russia were fighting over market share.

u15l2-2.prompt: Tap the lowest point in this period (weekly closes). (WTI oil · weekly closes · to 20/04/2020)
u15l2-2.explanation: The week of 20 April 2020 closed at about $17. The −$37.63 doesn't show up in weekly closes: it was a single day and a single contract, the May one, just before it expired.

u15l2-3.prompt: 20 April 2020: WTI has just hit negative prices. The roads are empty and there's almost nowhere left to store crude. What did oil do next?
u15l2-3.explanation: At that point hardly anyone dared to make forecasts: everything depended on when lockdowns would end and on OPEC+ cuts.

u15l2-4.prompt: March 2022: war breaks out in Ukraine and Brent soars. Pablo wants to buy oil company shares right now "because this can only go up". What do you tell him?
options: To sell everything he has in the stock market
To buy as much as he can
That the price already reflects the news and can turn quickly: he shouldn't decide based on headlines
u15l2-4.explanation: Commodities react very fast to geopolitics: by the time you read the headline, the price has already jumped.
feedback: One piece of news doesn't justify dismantling a whole portfolio.
Buying right at the peak out of euphoria is very risky: crude falls violently too (2008).
Good: after the March 2022 peak, crude fell sharply over the following months.

options: OPEC plus other producers such as Russia, who agree production quotas
u15l2-5.explanation: Since 2016 it has coordinated production across around twenty countries.

u15l2-6.prompt: Match each event with its usual effect on crude.
options: Inventories full and nowhere to store
right: Rises on fears of a supply cut

u15l2-7.prompt: On 20 April 2020, the May WTI contract closed at −$37.63: the seller was paying the buyer.
u15l2-7.explanation: People holding contracts about to expire had nowhere to store the crude and paid to get rid of them.

u15l2-8.prompt: Brent and WTI are priced in dollars per ____.

u15l2-9.prompt: A barrel holds about 159 litres. If Brent is at $80 and EUR/USD = 1.16, how much does a litre of crude cost in euros? (round to the cent)
u15l2-9.explanation: 80 ÷ 1.16 ≈ €68.97 per barrel; 68.97 ÷ 159 ≈ €0.43 per litre. The rest of the price of petrol is refining, transport, margins and taxes.

u15l2-10.prompt: Why does a strong euro make oil cheaper for Spain?
options: Because crude is paid for in dollars
Because Spain produces a lot of oil
u15l2-10.explanation: With more dollars per euro, the same barrel costs fewer euros.

u15l3-1.prompt: Match each commodity with what moves it most.
u15l3-1.explanation: Each commodity has its own main driver.
right: Harvests and conflicts in big exporters

u15l3-2.explanation: Metals depend on industry; agricultural commodities, on farming and the weather.

options: Because a medical body regulates it
Because it's widely used in hospitals
Because its price tends to anticipate how the economy is doing
u15l3-3.explanation: It's in almost everything that gets built and manufactured: if the economy speeds up or slows down, you see it in the price.

u15l3-4.prompt: Real chart of a metal (30 sessions, no name or date). What did it do over the next 10?
u15l3-4.explanation: Metals used both in industry and as investments are pushed by two forces at once, the economy and fear. That makes them very volatile.

u15l3-5.prompt: Another real metal, another 30 sessions. Up or down?
u15l3-5.explanation: A strong move one way doesn't tell you about the next: some metals move 10 % in a few weeks, in either direction.

u15l3-6.prompt: More than half of silver demand is industrial.
u15l3-6.explanation: In 2024, almost 60 %: electronics, solar panels… That's why silver usually suffers more than gold when the economy slows.

u15l3-7.prompt: Cocoa ended 2023 at about $4,200 a tonne and rose 178 % in 2024. Roughly where did it end 2024?
u15l3-7.explanation: 4,200 × 2.78 ≈ $11,676. In reality it ended 2024 at around $11,675 a tonne.

u15l3-8.prompt: A frost in Brazil threatens the coffee harvest. Marta runs a café in Valencia. What's most likely?
options: Coffee beans get more expensive and her costs go up
It won't affect her because she buys from a Spanish supplier
u15l3-8.explanation: With agricultural commodities, the weather in a big producer moves the global price.
feedback: That's it: less supply, higher price. In 2024 drought in Brazil pushed arabica to record highs.
A bad harvest reduces supply: normally the opposite happens.
Brazil is the world's biggest producer: the global price ends up reaching her supplier.

u15l3-9.prompt: Quick: which war sent the price of wheat soaring in 2022?
options: None, it was a pest outbreak
u15l3-9.explanation: Russia and Ukraine accounted for about 30 % of global wheat exports.

u15l3-10.prompt: What can push up the price of an agricultural commodity? Select all that apply.
options: A drought in a big producer
u15l3-10.explanation: A record harvest increases supply and usually lowers the price.

u15l4-1.prompt: Match each way of investing with its feature.
u15l4-1.explanation: Four routes with very different risks.
right: A contract with an expiry date and leverage
Depend on the metal and on how the company is run
Trades on an exchange and is backed by metal
You own the metal, but you have to store it

options: A listed product that tracks a commodity
u15l4-2.explanation: It trades on an exchange like an ETF, but tracks a commodity.

u15l4-3.prompt: A gold miner's share moves exactly like gold.
u15l4-3.explanation: It usually moves more, in both directions, because it has fixed costs and debt.

u15l4-4.prompt: A miner produces gold at a cost of $1,500 an ounce and sells it at $2,000. If gold rises 10 %, how much does its margin per ounce rise (in %)?
u15l4-4.explanation: Margin before: $500. With gold at $2,200: $700. (700 − 500) ÷ 500 = +40 %. That's why miners amplify what the metal does… on the way down too.

u15l4-5.prompt: Does it give you direct exposure to the price, or exposure through a company?
u15l4-5.explanation: With a company you're also buying its management, its debt and its costs.

u15l4-6.prompt: Physical gold ETCs usually have bars stored in a vault to back the product.
u15l4-6.explanation: That's why they track gold very closely, minus their small annual fee.

u15l4-7.prompt: Bruno wants to "invest in oil". He wants to understand properly what he's buying and not use leverage. Which option does he rule out first?
options: Leveraged WTI futures from an app
u15l4-7.explanation: Leveraged futures aren't for beginners: you can lose money very fast.
feedback: It's the easiest to understand, although it doesn't track the barrel exactly.
It's not the first one to rule out, but it has futures roll costs: he needs to understand them first.
That's it: leverage and expiry dates are exactly what he wants to avoid.

u15l4-8.prompt: Quick: which option means you have to store the metal yourself?
u15l4-8.explanation: You need a safe or have to pay for a custody service.

u15l4-9.prompt: What are the drawbacks of gold bars? Select all that apply.
options: The gap between buying and selling price can be large
You have to store and insure it
u15l4-9.explanation: Gold pays nothing; and buying and selling it physically has costs.

u15l4-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: That's CFDs or leveraged futures: a 10 % move against you wipes out everything, and promising profits is a bad sign
u15l4-10.explanation: At 1:10, a 10 % move against you takes you to zero. CFDs are complex instruments and come with a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage. Between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs.
feedback: OK, I'd better understand what an ETC is before touching anything leveraged.
At 1:10, a 10 % move against you wipes out everything. And promising 300 % is a red flag.
lines: I saw an ad: "Trade oil at 1:10 and make 300 % this month" 🛢️

u15l5-1.prompt: The June future is at $25 and the July one at $28. The curve is in…
u15l5-1.explanation: Later contracts dearer than nearer ones = contango.

u15l5-2.prompt: A fund has $1,000 in the May future, which is at $20. When it rolls, it sells at $20 and buys the June one, at $25. How many barrels does it control now?
u15l5-2.explanation: Before: 1,000 ÷ 20 = 50 barrels. After: 1,000 ÷ 25 = 40. In contango, every roll leaves you with fewer.

u15l5-3.prompt: Following on: the June future reaches expiry at $20, because crude hasn't moved. What's the fund worth now?
u15l5-3.explanation: 40 barrels × $20 = $800: −20 % without crude falling at all. That's the cost of contango.

u15l5-4.prompt: Tap WTI's highest point in this period (weekly closes). (WTI oil · weekly closes · to 20/04/2020)
u15l5-4.explanation: About $63 in January 2020. Three months later it was closing weeks below $20, and the May contract even traded in negative territory.

u15l5-5.prompt: Real oil chart: 30 sessions with no date. What did crude do over the next 10?
u15l5-5.explanation: Even if you got the direction of the barrel right, a futures fund in contango could make quite a bit less, or even lose money.

u15l5-6.prompt: An oil futures fund always tracks the barrel price you see in the news exactly.
u15l5-6.explanation: The one in the news is the near contract; the fund rolls contracts and pays (or earns) the difference along the curve.

u15l5-7.prompt: Match each term with its definition.
u15l5-7.explanation: With these four words you already understand why an oil fund doesn't track the barrel.
right: Selling the near contract and buying the next one
Later futures cost less than nearer ones
Later futures cost more than nearer ones

u15l5-8.prompt: April 2020. Ana sees crude on the floor and buys an oil futures fund "for when it recovers". What risk hasn't she looked at?
options: The cost of rolling futures in contango
None: if crude rises, she makes the same
The fund being priced in dollars
u15l5-8.explanation: With commodities, the product matters as much as the direction of the price.
feedback: Exactly: in 2020 USO lost about 68 % while spot WTI fell around 20 %.
With such steep contango, every roll costs her barrels: even if crude recovers, the fund can be left far behind.
It's a risk, but a small one compared with the contango at that time.

u15l5-9.explanation: You sell the near one dear and buy the later one cheap: with the same money you hold more barrels.

u15l5-10.prompt: A fund loses 68 %. How much does it then need to rise to get back to where it started?
u15l5-10.explanation: 1 ÷ 0.32 = 3.125 → it needs +212.5 %. Big falls are extremely hard to recover from.
